documents.unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
documents.title: Generative AI in Teaching and Learning
documents.summary: UConn's teaching center states that the university has no blanket AI policy and makes instructors responsible for setting course and assignment expectations. The page recommends what a syllabus statement should cover, recommends but does not require Copilot, warns against detection software and entering protected data, and mostly offers pedagogy resources and workshop listings.
documents.stance_why: The page says "The university does not have a blanket AI policy" and that "instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations", so it sets no stance itself and delegates; it gives syllabus advice but no named tiers or templates.

units.why: "The university does not have a blanket AI policy" states that no single university-wide rule exists, which leaves the decision below the university, so I assign P04 (who decides) and not a stance type.
units.anchor: The university does not have a blanket AI policy.
units.fit_note: Reports that there is no university-wide rule; the explicit hand-off to instructors is in the next sentence.

units.why: "AI use is governed by the Data Classification Policy, the ... Integrity and Misconduct Policy, and ... FERPA" ties AI use to existing policy and law, which is P77 (comply with existing law and policy).
units.anchor: AI use is governed by the Data Classification Policy
units.policy: AI use is governed by the Data Classification Policy, the Academic, Scholarly, and Professional Integrity and Misconduct Policy, and FERPA.

units.why: "instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations" assigns the decision to instructors, which is P04; it binds instructors, and is set before the course.
units.anchor: instructors are responsible for setting and communicating their own course- and assignment-level expectations

units.why: "There is no single approach appropriate for every course, discipline, or assignment" justifies per-instructor rules. P04 fits because it explains why the rule varies; it is a rationale, so modality is informs.
units.anchor: There is no single approach appropriate for every course, discipline, or assignment.

units.why: Says "what counts as 'using AI' is not always obvious to students" because tools range from autofill to chatbots. It is a scoping point about what AI covers, so P61 (define AI and scope); it implies rules should be explicit.
units.anchor: Generative AI tools themselves range from simple autofill in emails

units.why: Defines generative AI: "Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a technology for conversational information searches that ... can create original content". A definition that sets what the guidance covers is P61.
units.anchor: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a technology for conversational information searches

units.why: Cites a study: "30 percent of students reported using generative AI and more than fifty percent reported positive attitudes". This is evidence about student AI use and attitudes, closest to P55 though it is not about learning effects.
units.anchor: 30 percent of students reported using generative AI
units.fit_note: Cites prevalence of and attitudes toward student AI use, not evidence on how AI affects learning or performance.

units.why: "There is confusion ... about which professors allow AI ... students may either avoid using AI entirely or use it inappropriately" gives the reason clear expectations are needed. No type covers a stated problem of student confusion over rules.
units.anchor: There is confusion, however, about which professors allow AI to be used in projects
units.uncovered_note: Names student confusion about which instructors allow AI and where collaboration ends and cheating begins as the reason expectations must be clear.

units.why: "We recommend your syllabus statement address:" followed by a list tells instructors to put AI expectations in the syllabus. The verb "recommend" makes it should; it is P09 (AI statement in the syllabus).
units.anchor: We recommend your syllabus statement address:

units.why: The first list item, "what uses of generative AI are permitted and what uses are not, including whether that differs by assignment", asks the syllabus to state permitted and barred uses per assignment. P09 since it is about what the statement covers; P04 also fits but the rule here is to write it down.
units.anchor: what uses of generative AI are permitted and what uses are not, including whether

units.why: "whether any use is required, and for what purpose" asks instructors to state in the syllabus if AI use is required. P09 because it is a syllabus content item; the requirement itself (P79) is not imposed here.
units.anchor: whether any use is required, and for what purpose;

units.why: "what AI tools students are required to purchase or access, including any cost or account requirements" asks for cost and account requirements to be stated. P51 (equity and cost) is the nearest type, but the rule is a syllabus disclosure item.
units.anchor: what AI tools students are required to purchase or access, including any cost or
units.fit_note: Asks instructors to disclose required tools, costs and accounts; it does not say paid tools must not be required.

units.why: "what disclosure or acknowledgment of AI use you expect" tells instructors to state their disclosure expectation in the syllabus. P24 is the home for disclosure, though here the rule is on the instructor to specify it.
units.anchor: what disclosure or acknowledgment of AI use you expect;
units.fit_note: Does not require students to disclose; it asks instructors to say what disclosure they expect.

units.why: "what will happen if a student uses AI outside your stated expectations" asks instructors to state consequences up front. P37 (state penalties in advance) matches.
units.anchor: what will happen if a student uses AI outside your stated expectations
units.fit_note: Asks only that consequences be stated, without naming any specific penalty.

units.why: "how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn" ties the AI rules to learning goals, which is P83 (align AI decisions with learning objectives).
units.anchor: how these expectations connect to what students are meant to learn.

units.why: "You may also want to tell students whether and how you use generative AI yourself" is optional advice (may) that instructors disclose their own AI use, which is P47.
units.anchor: You may also want to tell students whether and how you use generative AI yourself

units.why: "Being clear about this, one way or the other, helps build trust and avoids misunderstandings" gives the reason for telling students about instructor AI use. Part of the P47 advice, kept as a separate rationale.
units.anchor: helps build trust and avoids misunderstandings
units.fit_note: States a trust rationale for transparency; it is not itself an instruction to disclose.

units.why: "For sample AI syllabus statements you can adapt directly ... expand the section below" points instructors to ready-made syllabus language. It supports the syllabus-statement expectation, so P09.
units.anchor: sample AI syllabus statements you can adapt directly
units.fit_note: Offers sample statements to adapt rather than requiring a statement.

units.why: "Including AI or addressing it with your students will help prepare them for jobs or further work" argues for teaching with AI as preparation for work, which is P44 (teach effective AI use as a professional skill).
units.anchor: will help prepare them for jobs or further work in most disciplines

units.why: "Please reach out to CETL for 1:1 consultations on integrating AI into activities and assignments" offers consultation to instructors, which is P63 (support faculty in learning AI).
units.anchor: Please reach out to CETL for 1:1 consultations on integrating AI

units.why: Lists "The foundations of AI literacy" (knowing when to use AI, prompting, critically evaluating output, conceptual understanding, identifying risks). It names what AI literacy teaching should cover, so P70 (AI literacy) fits partly.
units.anchor: The foundations of AI literacy are:
units.fit_note: Defines the components of AI literacy for instructors to build into courses; the guidance does not offer or mandate a training.

units.why: "Critically evaluating AI output" is listed as a foundation of AI literacy; it expects students to learn to check AI output, matching P31 (verify AI output).
units.anchor: Critically evaluating AI output
units.fit_note: Appears as an AI-literacy competency in a list, not as a rule that students must verify what they submit.

units.why: "Knowing how to ask and refine questions with an AI chatbot (\"prompting\")" is named as an AI-literacy foundation. The content is advice about prompting effectively, which is P93.
units.anchor: Knowing how to ask and refine questions with an AI chatbot
units.fit_note: A listed competency rather than concrete prompt advice.

units.why: "UConn has a contract with Microsoft for basic access to Copilot. It is free to faculty, staff, and students." The university provides a licensed tool free of charge, which P92 (use university-licensed tools) covers; the free access also relates to P51.
units.anchor: UConn has a contract with Microsoft for basic access to Copilot.

units.why: "the contract affords privacy protections and includes an agreement that queries will not be used to train large language models" gives the privacy reason to prefer the licensed tool, which is P50.
units.anchor: the contract affords privacy protections and includes an agreement that queries will not be

units.why: "it is recommended, though not required, that you use Copilot" is a soft preference for the university-licensed tool (should). P92 is the home since the tool is institution-wide, not course-specific.
units.anchor: it is recommended, though not required, that you use Copilot.

units.why: "all university employees should make sure to avoid using any software, including AI platforms, for anything to do with protected university data. This includes FERPA-protected student information." Protects data, binds employees, so P50 with should-not as the strongest fitting modality.
units.anchor: avoid using any software, including AI platforms, for anything to do with protected university data

units.why: "This includes FERPA-protected student information" extends the protected-data rule to student records; it is a separate named category and falls under P50.
units.anchor: This includes FERPA-protected student information.

units.why: "This industry changes constantly, with new tools being added, enhanced, or removed" explains why the guidance cannot be fixed; closest is P54 (policy will be revisited), although it speaks about tools, not the policy.
units.anchor: This industry changes constantly, with new tools being added, enhanced, or removed.
units.fit_note: Says the tool landscape changes, not that the policy will be revised.

units.why: "Understand FERPA and follow UConn's Data Classification Policy" is a practice instructors should follow when choosing and working with a tool. It reinforces existing policy, P77; the privacy substance is also P50.
units.anchor: Understand FERPA and follow

units.why: "Connect the choice to your course learning objectives" tells instructors to base the choice of AI tool on learning goals, which is P83.
units.anchor: Connect the choice to your course learning objectives

units.why: "Transparently communicate to students your definition of plagiarism and cheating" asks instructors to state what counts as misuse in their course. P09 (state expectations) fits; P36 is about classifying misuse, which this does not do.
units.anchor: Transparently communicate to students your definition of plagiarism and cheating
units.fit_note: Asks for communication of the instructor's definition of plagiarism and cheating, not specifically an AI statement in the syllabus.

units.why: "Communicate to students the risks of AI" asks instructors to tell students about AI risks, i.e. explain the stakes beyond listing the rule, which is P66.
units.anchor: Communicate to students the risks of AI

units.why: "Require students to demonstrate comprehension of what is 'identifiable information' so they can avoid entering it into an AI tool" has instructors require students to show they know what not to enter. P50 (protect personal data) fits.
units.anchor: so they can avoid entering it into an AI tool

units.why: "Currently detection software is of limited use and may be detrimental because it generates false negatives and ... false positives" says detectors are unreliable, which is P39.
units.anchor: detection software is of limited use and may be detrimental

units.why: "At best, an AI detector would only ever provide a likelihood of AI-generated text, not a definitive determination" says detector output is not proof. P39 (do not rely on detectors) fits; P69 covers evidence standards but this is mainly a reliability claim.
units.anchor: not a definitive determination

units.why: "UConn does not currently license any AI detection software, and similar functionality is not available in SafeAssign" states the university provides no detector, so none is relied on. P39.
units.anchor: UConn does not currently license any AI detection software

units.why: "CETL continues to review and evaluate them" says detection tools will be re-evaluated as they develop. A commitment to revisit, so P54.
units.anchor: CETL continues to review and evaluate them
units.fit_note: Commits to re-evaluating detection tools, not the policy as a whole.

units.why: The Copyright Office "published guidance on copyright in January 2025" is pointed to in the discussion of AI and copyright. A reference to copyright of AI material, so P52, though no rule is stated.
units.anchor: published guidance on copyright in January 2025
units.fit_note: Only points to external copyright guidance without stating a rule.

units.why: "Require students to slow down, engage as active readers, and reflect on their engagement with these tools" asks instructors to build reflection on AI use into the course. Students keep reflections on use: P26.
units.anchor: reflect on their engagement with these tools
units.fit_note: Recommends that instructors require reflection; it does not itself make students keep or submit transcripts.

units.why: "You could ask students to use this Template and rubric for students to track their use of AI ... and perhaps assign points to doing so" suggests a tracking template graded with points. P26 for tracking, with the grading element as P35.
units.anchor: Template and rubric for students to track their use of AI
units.fit_note: Also suggests awarding points for tracking, which is an assignment-design element.

units.why: "Make sure you communicate to students that this work supports the course learning objectives" tells instructors to explain why the tracking task exists, which is P66.
units.anchor: communicate to students that this work supports the course learning objectives

units.why: The "AI marble layer cake" approach "incorporates AI into both homework and in-class work" with class time analyzing AI output. It is an assignment redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: incorporates AI into both homework and in-class work

units.why: The "AI sandwich" has "students use AI as a brainstorming partner first, then spend time with other students in class ... and finally use AI again as a writing partner." A sequenced redesign with AI for brainstorming and writing support; P35 as the course-structure type.
units.anchor: students use AI as a brainstorming partner first
units.fit_note: Also permits AI for brainstorming and as a writing partner (P15, P91) within the redesigned sequence.

units.why: "Please consult the UConn Office of Community Standards and the university's academic misconduct policy for information about handling plagiarism and cheating" sends instructors to the formal integrity process, P81.
units.anchor: Please consult the UConn Office of Community Standards
units.fit_note: Refers instructors to the office and policy without stating procedural steps.

units.why: "cheating and plagiarism often stem from reasons other than lack of ethics" names causes of misuse (unclear collaboration norms, overload from courses, jobs or family). P99 (reduce pressures that lead to misuse) is the closest type; the response itself (P68) is not stated.
units.anchor: cheating and plagiarism often stem from reasons other than lack of ethics
units.fit_note: Names causes of misuse but does not itself prescribe extensions or support.

units.why: "There is a lot we can do, pedagogically, to scaffold assignments, make content accessible, and communicate the value and purpose of using generative AI critically and judiciously" urges instructors to ease the pressures behind misuse by scaffolding and explaining purpose. P99 for prevention; P66 is the second candidate, but scaffolding is the main action.
units.anchor: scaffold assignments, make content accessible, and communicate the value and purpose

units.why: The MIT toolkit "walks you through ... mapping AI activities onto your course learning objectives; and finally scaffolding related activities" to secure assessment reliability. A resource for redesigning assessment around AI, P35.
units.anchor: mapping AI activities onto your course learning objectives

units.why: Describes using AI "to help you create Pre and Post Class Surveys to gather baseline data about your students' needs". It is an instructor use of AI for teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: method for using AI to help you create

units.why: "CETL continues to prioritize programming that creates learning communities across the university" describes ongoing faculty programming on AI, which is P63.
units.anchor: CETL continues to prioritize programming that creates learning communities across the university

units.why: "the challenges and benefits of AI will be realized within departments and shaped by disciplinary norms" says AI practice is set at the department and discipline level. P85 (units set their own rules) fits partly.
units.anchor: will be realized within departments and shaped by disciplinary norms of inquiry
units.fit_note: Acknowledges disciplinary and departmental variation without giving units authority to set rules.

units.why: "CETL organizes learning communities and workshops where UConn faculty, staff and students can gain awareness, learn foundational skills, and get support for creating syllabus policies" describes AI learning opportunities open to the community, P70; the faculty support aspect is P63.
units.anchor: CETL organizes learning communities and workshops where UConn faculty, staff and students

units.why: "The resources on this page will be updated continuously" shows a living page that will be revisited. P54 (revisit regularly).
units.anchor: The resources on this page will be updated continuously.

units.why: "Last reviewed: August 2026" records when the guidance was last reviewed; it is a date of review rather than a process, so I treat it as P84 (how and when the guidance was made).
units.anchor: Last reviewed: August 2026
units.fit_note: A review date only, with no description of process or body.

units.why: The Graduate School session will review the ASPIM Policy "to foster greater understanding of how to report Scholarly Misconduct, with a focus on ASPIM when AI use is suspected." A reporting route for suspected AI misuse: P81.
units.anchor: how to report Scholarly Misconduct, with a focus on ASPIM when AI use is suspected
units.fit_note: Workshop description that signals a reporting route for suspected AI misuse; no steps are given.

units.why: A workshop will "explore the impact of AI use through the lens of equitable access and fairness", including restrictions on non-native English-speaking scholars. It raises an equity concern about restrictions, P51, as an informs item.
units.anchor: equitable access and fairness in higher education
units.fit_note: Names equity of AI restrictions for non-native English speakers as a topic; states no rule.

units.why: A workshop offers ideas for "using GenAI to edit assignment prompts for clarity, create case studies, generate problem sets, develop remedial modules, and make quizzes". Instructor AI use for teaching work: P59.
units.anchor: using GenAI to edit assignment prompts for clarity, create case studies, generate problem sets

units.why: A Library workshop presents AI tools "as an academic research partner" for literature reviews and citation management. It promotes AI for research tasks; P62 governs AI in research and scholarship and is the nearest type.
units.anchor: Explore the potential of AI as an academic research partner
units.fit_note: Promotes AI tools for research tasks; it is a workshop, not a rule about AI in research or scholarship.

units.why: A session asks "Are you considering requiring students to use AI in a course project or assignment?" and shares a case study of ChatGPT in a major project. It supports instructors who build AI into coursework, P79.
units.anchor: requiring students to use AI in a course project or assignment
units.fit_note: A workshop prompt that treats required AI use as an option for instructors; no rule.

units.why: The "AI Safety Literacy" workshop is "designed for faculty and instructors across disciplines who want to develop a foundational understanding of advanced AI systems and their potential impacts". Faculty learning about AI risk: P63.
units.anchor: designed for faculty and instructors across disciplines who want to develop a foundational understanding

units.why: The "Developing Student AI Fluencies" series teaches "activities to promote student critical thinking about the output of large language models". It helps instructors teach AI literacy to students: P70, with faculty audience.
units.anchor: activities to promote student critical thinking about the output of large language models
units.fit_note: Audience is faculty learning to teach AI fluency; P63 would also fit.

units.why: The Community Standards session covers "Setting Clear Expectations: ... establishing course guidelines regarding the use of AI tools to promote transparency and fairness." It supports instructors in writing course AI guidelines: P63.
units.anchor: establishing course guidelines regarding the use of AI tools to promote transparency and fairness

units.why: The same session will "Review relevant university data on the impact and prevalence of AI tool usage in cases referred for academic misconduct." Evidence about AI in misconduct cases: P55.
units.anchor: university data on the impact and prevalence of AI tool usage in cases referred
units.fit_note: Data are about prevalence in misconduct referrals, not on learning effects.

units.why: A workshop on the "Blackboard AI Design Assistant" shows how it "can simplify course development". An instructor use of AI for course development: P59.
units.anchor: Blackboard AI Design Assistant can simplify course development

units.why: "Detection of AI use will not be the focus of these sessions, but we may discuss AI-resistant activities and assignments" says the workshops focus on teaching with AI rather than catching it. It is not a statement that staff will not police AI (P60), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Detection of AI use will not be the focus of these sessions
units.uncovered_note: States the workshop emphasis is not detection; not a statement that staff will not police AI.

notes: Only one included document (CETL page). The sample syllabus statements section was not present in the saved text, so none were coded. Past workshop listings were coded only where they state a position or offer; repeated listings were not recoded.
